title: Sixty-Four Unread
text: The report is due at 5. Your inbox has 64 unread, nine flagged urgent and one titled "Quick question" that is not quick. Your toddler has brought you a shoe and would like you to wear it on your head while you work.

choices.label: Wear the shoe. Answer emails one-handed.

outcomes.text: You clear 31 emails with a sneaker on your head, then forget it's there for your next call. Nobody says anything. Someone in Finance reacts with a single 👟.

choices.label: Mark all 64 as read. Fresh start.

outcomes.text: One click. It feels incredible, like a cold shower for your brain. Two of the 64 were from daycare. One said you're bringing snacks for Thursday. You are now bringing snacks for Thursday.

choices.label: Ask your partner to take the toddler until lunch

outcomes.text: They close their laptop, pick up the toddler and the shoe, and go. You answer emails like a machine built for it. They don't say "you owe me." They don't have to.
"I have the all-hands at 10." They do. They've mentioned it four times this week. You both stand in the hallway holding opposite ends of the same tiredness.

title: The Afternoon Wall
text: The report needs two more hours of brain. You have about twenty minutes of brain left. The coffee maker sits on the counter, humming softly, like it already knows how this ends.

choices.label: Fourth coffee. Tonight is tomorrow's problem.

outcomes.text: You type with the focus of a jewel thief and the pulse of a hummingbird. The report jumps to 80%. At 11 PM you'll be wide awake, explaining it to your partner, who is asleep.

choices.label: Ask your partner to take the toddler for an hour

outcomes.text: They take the toddler to the park. You write in a silent house, then sit very still for six minutes, listening to the fridge. It sounds like the ocean.
"I've got a 3:30." It's on the shared calendar, in the color you agreed was theirs. You write the rest with a toddler braiding yogurt into your hair.

choices.label: Cold water on the face. Finish it on fumes.

outcomes.text: It's good, actually. You'd celebrate, but standing up makes the room tilt like a boat, so you celebrate sitting down, quietly, with a cracker.

title: Due at 5
text: The report is 80% done and 100% due at 5. Your toddler has found the laptop's power button. It glows. They love it. Every time they touch it, you make a sound you didn't know you could make.

choices.label: Power through, toddler on your lap

outcomes.text: You type with your arms out like a T. rex so they fit in the gap. Submitted at 4:58. On page 6 there's a "jjjjjjjjj" you won't find until the meeting about it.

choices.label: Sunshine Sing-Along. Twenty-two minutes. Go.

outcomes.text: The man in corduroy sings about sharing. You write like the building is on fire. Submitted at 4:31, which is early, which nobody will ever notice.

choices.label: Send it at 80%. "Happy to discuss!"

outcomes.text: "Happy to discuss!" is corporate for "I know." Your manager replies "Thanks!" and nothing else. You will think about that exclamation point all night.

title: Cabin Fever
text: Daycare is closed until the class is "symptom-free." You've read the truck book 19 times today. You've built the same tower 31 times so it could be knocked down 31 times. The walls are getting closer.

choices.label: Build a blanket fort. Commit to the bit.

outcomes.text: Four chairs, every blanket you own and a flashlight. Inside, your toddler whispers like you're both hiding from someone. You stay in there much longer than you meant to.

choices.label: Sunshine Sing-Along. Just one.

outcomes.text: The man in corduroy sings about rainy days. You eat crackers over the kitchen sink, standing up, which is your version of a spa day.

choices.label: "Quiet time. You play, I sit."

outcomes.text: They play beside you, narrating everything, for fourteen whole minutes. You sit. You don't talk. It's the best meeting you've had all week.
Quiet time lasts 90 seconds, then becomes loud time, on your lap, with a drum.

title: Wash Everything on Hot
text: The daycare email says to wash "all bedding, towels and soft toys" on hot. Mr. Blanket is a soft toy. Mr. Blanket has never been washed. Mr. Blanket has a smell your toddler describes as "home."

choices.label: Every load. Mr. Blanket too.

outcomes.text: Four loads. Your toddler watches Mr. Blanket tumble in the dryer window like a hostage video. He comes out warm, clean and, according to your toddler, "wrong."

choices.label: Text your partner: laundry tonight is theirs

outcomes.text: "On it." Four loads after bedtime, folded, Mr. Blanket included. You find him on your pillow at 10 PM, still warm. You are not crying. It's the steam.
"I did laundry Sunday." It was one load, of their gym clothes. You don't say that. You think it, at a volume they can probably hear.

choices.label: Just the sheets. Mr. Blanket stays feral.

outcomes.text: Sheets on hot. Mr. Blanket stays fragrant and untouched. If daycare ever asks, he was washed, and you will lie to a teacher's face.

title: Is That Eye Pink?
text: Your toddler rubs one eye. You freeze. You hold their face under the kitchen light like a jeweler with a stolen diamond. It looks eye-colored? Probably? You've stared so long you've forgotten what eyes look like.

choices.label: Call the nurse line, just to be sure

outcomes.text: The nurse asks four calm questions. No redness, no goop, no fever. "Sounds like a tired eye." Your toddler says "hi" to the nurse eleven times. You thank them like someone pulled from the sea.

choices.label: Text your partner a close-up: "PINK??"

outcomes.text: "Looks like an eye. A very cute eye." Ten minutes later: "Called the nurse line from the stairwell. Tired eye. We're fine." You read "we're" four times.
"?" Then "looks fine??" Then "in a meeting." Three texts, two question marks, no help. You call the nurse line yourself, slightly louder than you need to.

choices.label: Post it to the group chat for a vote

outcomes.text: Eleven parents vote. Six say pink, four say fine, one sends a link to an eye oil. The daycare director has seen it now. The director has questions about tomorrow.

title: The Bite
text: Mid-cuddle, your toddler bites your shoulder. Not a nibble. A full, molar-assisted chomp, with eye contact. Then a giggle, because your face just did something it has never done before.

choices.label: Calmly: "Ouch. Teeth are for the teether."

outcomes.text: You swap your shoulder for a cold teether and say it like a nature documentary. They chomp the teether instead. Lesson received, for the next ten minutes.
They bite the teether, then you, then the teether, as if comparing. You come in second. It stings in a whole new way.

choices.label: Make a big, wounded noise

outcomes.text: It is the funniest thing that has ever happened. They bite again for an encore. The encore is mostly [BLEEP]. You are now a squeaky toy with a mortgage.

choices.label: Frozen teether and a pouch. Buy some peace.

outcomes.text: One cold ring, one $2.99 pouch. Silence, chewing, a small sigh from you both. Then the pouch gets squeezed into the couch. Your shoulder has a perfect dental record on it.

title: Bib Number Seven
text: Bib number seven. The drool is industrial. Your toddler's chin is red and chapped, your shoulder is damp, and the couch has a wet patch the shape of a small country.

choices.label: Chin balm after every wipe

outcomes.text: You apply balm 11 times. By the eleventh, they lift their chin for it, like a tiny boxer between rounds. The red fades. Your respect for boxing trainers grows.

choices.label: Text your partner: more bibs, the good balm

outcomes.text: They get home with bibs, balm and a frozen teething ring they bought without being asked. You consider proposing again.
"What kind of bibs?" "The bib kind." They get home with one bib. It has a lobster on it. It says "Shell Yeah." Technically, a bib.

choices.label: Let it drip. You live in a swamp now.

outcomes.text: You stop fighting it. Everything you own is slightly damp. The couch patch is now a large country, with a coastline.

title: Grandma Has Posted
text: Grandma has posted 41 photos of today. Number 23 is the toddler eating spaghetti with both fists, captioned "Somebody's parents let them eat like THIS 😂." It has 88 likes. Three are from the group chat.

choices.label: Call her. Ask her to take that one down.

outcomes.text: She takes it down. She posts a new one: "Not allowed to share the spaghetti one 🙄." It has more likes than the spaghetti did.
"Of course, sweetheart," she says, and takes it down, in a voice so sincere you check it for traps. There are no traps. You're too tired to trust that.

choices.label: Comment: "Best day ever!! ❤️❤️❤️"

outcomes.text: Spin control. Two parents like your comment. One replies "lol the spaghetti 😂." You have made it a thread. Threads are forever.

choices.label: Screenshot it to your partner

outcomes.text: "LOL. Honestly, the spaghetti looks great." A small, private laugh between the two people who actually run this place.
"Well, did you let them eat like that?" You did. They know you did. You put the phone face-down, very gently, like it might go off.

title: "Oh, You Cut Them THAT Way"
text: At dinner, Grandma watches your partner cut the toddler's noodles into small, sensible pieces. "Oh," she says, to no one, to everyone. "You cut them THAT way." The knife stops.

choices.label: "They cut them perfectly."

outcomes.text: Grandma raises both hands, the picture of innocence. The knife resumes. Later, Grandma tells the family group chat you've been "very sensitive lately."

choices.label: Laugh along. They do cut them a bit small.

outcomes.text: Grandma beams. Your partner's knife stays very still. You will hear about this at 10:40 PM, in a whisper, in the dark.

choices.label: Ask Grandma about her knee. All of it.

outcomes.text: Thirty minutes on the knee: the surgeon, the parking, the physical therapist who "isn't a real doctor." Your partner finishes dinner in peace and squeezes your hand under the table.

title: Sticker Inflation
text: The deal was one sticker per potty. Your toddler has renegotiated: two stickers, a cracker and "the big song." The chart on the fridge now looks like a bank in a history documentary.

choices.label: Hold the line: one sticker, no song

outcomes.text: They accept the terms, sulk, and go anyway. One sticker. You feel like a central banker who did the hard thing.
They go on strike. The strike takes place on the kitchen floor, with eye contact.

choices.label: Two stickers and a cracker. Inflation is real.

outcomes.text: It works too well. They now go in tiny installments, for maximum stickers. Nine before lunch. You're out of dinosaurs and down to the dentist's smiley faces.

choices.label: Full potty parade for every success

outcomes.text: You march. You sing. You play a kazoo you didn't know you owned. They're so into it they go twice. You're so into it you pull something in your hip.

title: Bare-Bottom Afternoon
text: The method says: no pants, lots of water, watch for "the signs." Your toddler is pantsless, hydrated and showing the signs either constantly or never. You've watched a small bottom for 40 minutes like a lighthouse keeper.

choices.label: Keep watching. Potty every 20 minutes.

outcomes.text: Ding. Sprint. Success! You cheer so loudly a dog two houses down joins in. Your toddler takes a bow, which, given the outfit, is a lot.
Between dings: the couch. The good couch. Twelve seconds after the last trip, with total confidence.

choices.label: Sunshine Sing-Along. Stillness helps, right?

outcomes.text: The man in corduroy sings about rain. Your toddler sits perfectly still on the couch. Stillness, it turns out, is exactly when it happens. The cushion cover goes in the wash.

choices.label: Towels on every surface. Every one.

outcomes.text: Fourteen towels. The living room looks like a spa run by raccoons. It works: everything lands on terry cloth. You now have fourteen towels to wash.

title: The Sitter Has a Few Questions
text: The sitter texts: "Hi!! Few q's for tonight 😊" Then eleven questions, numbered. Number 7 is "do u have snacks for me." Number 11 is "Anything else I should know?" There is so much else.

choices.label: Write the full guide. Two pages. Bullet points.

outcomes.text: Routine, snacks, the Song (lyrics attached), where the backup lovey hides, what "the blue thing" means. The sitter replies "omg ur so organized." You're not. You're terrified.

choices.label: Answer number 7. The rest is vibes.

outcomes.text: "Snacks in the pantry. They'll be asleep. They may tell you about a bird." The sitter replies "ok!" with an energy you'll think about during dessert.

choices.label: Ask your partner to call the sitter

outcomes.text: They call. They go through all eleven and add a twelfth about the nightlight. You hear them say "we" a lot. You like hearing them say it.
"Can you? You know the routine." They're not wrong. That's the trap with the routine: you're the one who knows it. You answer all eleven, plus a twelfth nobody asked.

title: The Going-Out Shirt
text: Your going-out shirt has been in a drawer since spring. It has a crease like a folded map, a stain like a smaller map and, as of four minutes ago, a toddler wearing it as a cape.

choices.label: Iron it properly. Treat the stain. Be a person.

outcomes.text: Stain stick, steam, a second pass. It looks almost new, in low light, which the restaurant will provide. You hold it up like a trophy you ironed yourself.

choices.label: Dryer, damp towel, ten minutes. Pray.

outcomes.text: The crease is 60% gone. The stain is now baked in, a permanent feature. You'll keep an arm over it all night like a nervous senator.

choices.label: Wear the sweater. The sweater is always fine.

outcomes.text: The sweater has seen four Fridays like this one. Your partner will say "The sweater, huh?" in a voice that's either fond or not. You won't ask which.

title: Reservation Confirmed
text: Your partner texts: "Confirmed for 7:30!! 🎉" Then: "I could leave work at 3:30 so you can rest? I'd have to log back on later, but." The "but" just sits there. It's a real offer. It's also a real but.

choices.label: "Yes. Please. Come home."

outcomes.text: They're home by 4. You lie in a dark room for 40 minutes like a phone on a charger. When you get up, the toddler has "helped" fold laundry, which means unfolded it.
They're home at 4:40 and back on the laptop by 4:45. "I'm here, though!" they say, from behind a screen. Technically, they are.

choices.label: "I've got it. Finish your day."

outcomes.text: You've got it. You absolutely have it. At 4:30 you're on the floor looking for a shoe, and you have it, and your partner sends a heart, and that has to count for something.
